h1:
Hat Yai Fried Chicken
10 Spots Locals Actually Eat At
intro: Hat Yai fried chicken is the kind of food people fly in for and still feel it was worth the trip for a single plate. The magic is in the golden, crispy skin, meat marinated deep with southern spices, then showered with crunchy fried shallots — eaten with hot sticky rice and a punchy dipping sauce. But search around and you'll find endless shops, so which ones do Hat Yai locals actually eat at, not just the ones tourists photograph? We picked the 10 with the strongest, most consistent reviews from people who live here, with the area, price per piece, opening hours and what's worth ordering — no overhyping.
chips: 📍 Si Uthit · Kim Yong · Khlong Rian

blocks.html: Hat Yai fried chicken isn't the battered, breaded kind you might be used to. What sets it apart is the meat marinated with southern spices and herbs until the flavor soaks all the way through — some shops barely use any batter at all, so it comes out with crispy skin but the meat still juicy, not dry. Then it's topped with crunchy fried shallots, which are really the star of the plate, and served with sticky rice and a punchy dipping sauce. The difference between shops comes down to the marinade, how bold the seasoning is, and which cut they do best. We've ranked these by local popularity plus consistency of flavor — not just by how many views they get on social media.

blocks.title: How to read this ranking
blocks.html: A lower spot on the list doesn't mean a shop isn't good — fried chicken is purely a matter of taste. Someone who loves a bold, salty hit and someone who prefers a milder, easy-eating version will pick different shops. So we spell out what each one does best, to make it easier to land on the shop that suits your own palate.

blocks.text: 10 Hat Yai Fried Chicken Shops, Ranked

items.name: Decha Fried Chicken (Si Uthit)
items.blurb: One of the busiest shops in Hat Yai and usually the first name locals bring up. Open for over 30 years, the chicken is fragrant, the meat soft and juicy rather than dry, the skin golden and crispy, and it comes with a big pile of fried shallots. The other must-order is the strong, frothy pulled tea — pair it with warm sticky rice and you've got a perfect combo. It's right on Si Uthit Road and easy to find, so it's a great first stop if you've just arrived in Hat Yai.
items.meta: Si Uthit Road, city center · roughly 10:00–21:30
items.price: Sticky rice & fried chicken set ~69 THB

items.name: Hat Yai Meena Fried Chicken (Kim Yong Market)
items.blurb: A long-running shop in front of Kim Yong Market that's perfect to drop into while you're browsing for souvenirs. The flavor is bold, the dipping sauce excellent, and the sticky rice and fried shallots are generous. There are tables to sit and eat in, and it's clean and tidy. You can choose small, cheaper wings or big thigh-and-drumstick pieces. The location right in the shopping district makes it super convenient if you're staying near Kim Yong Market.
items.meta: In front of Kim Yong Market · 10:00–19:30 daily

items.name: Bang Jane Fried Chicken (Halal · Khlong Rian)
items.blurb: A legendary fried chicken name in Hat Yai, selling for over 30 years, and a halal shop locals rate among the very best. The standout is crispy skin, soft meat, and a clear garlic aroma, with a well-balanced marinade. It's near Khlong Rian Market and has been eaten by both Muslim and non-Muslim customers across generations. If you're after the original old-school flavor, this one's worth a try.
items.meta: Khlong Rian Market area · halal shop

items.name: Sofiya Fried Chicken (Si Uthit)
items.blurb: A pushcart shop diagonally across from Decha on Si Uthit Road, a longtime local favorite. It opens in the late afternoon and sells for a short window. The flavor is bold and deep into the spices, the marinade really soaks in, the fried shallots are great, and the dipping sauce is zingy. There's also khao mok (spiced rice) and chicken kolae to add on. The catch: it opens in the evening and often sells out fast, so if you've got your heart set on this one, go right when it opens.
items.meta: Si Uthit Road (pushcart) · opens around 15:30 onward

items.name: Pee Pla Sticky Rice & Fried Chicken (behind Hat Yai Hospital)
items.blurb: A legendary shop behind Hat Yai Hospital, just before the post office intersection. Locals queue so heavily you have to take a number ticket. Open for 20-plus years, the chicken is well marinated, slightly on the salty side, the meat not dry, the skin crispy, with its own distinctive dipping sauce — perfect with hot sticky rice and fried shallots. Prices are easy on the wallet. This is an everyday eating spot for Hat Yai people more than a photo stop.
items.meta: Behind Hat Yai Hospital, near the post office intersection · queue tickets

items.name: Sarina Fried Chicken (Greenway Market)
items.blurb: A shop in Greenway Market that reviewers praise for the cleanness of its spices and herbs — no bitter aftertaste on the tongue. The meat is soft, the skin crispy and fragrant, and it goes well with sticky rice. They do thighs fried a touch dry for extra crunch. A solid choice if you're staying or wandering the markets around Greenway and don't want to drive into the inner city.
items.meta: Greenway Market · open in the evening

items.name: Wanita Fried Chicken (Chue Chang night market)
items.blurb: A shop in the Chue Chang night-market area in front of a 7-Eleven, known for value and easy snacking. It fries up crispy but not greasy, with a natural herby aroma, and there are tiny, very cheap sticky rice parcels to eat alongside. Great to grab while strolling at night or to take back to the hotel — this is the kind of street fried chicken Hat Yai people eat as a late-night meal.
items.meta: Chue Chang night market (in front of 7-Eleven) · dinner to late night
items.price: ~20 THB per piece / sticky rice parcel ~10 THB

items.name: Malee Hat Yai Fried Chicken (Si Trang Market)
items.blurb: A shop in Si Trang Market that people in the area eat at regularly. It stands out for a distinctively fragrant marinade, and the meat comes out a bit drier and crispier — good for those who like fried chicken that isn't too juicy. Easy to grab in the market and the prices are friendly. It suits a breakfast-to-late-morning bite for anyone out shopping at Si Trang Market.
items.meta: Si Trang Market · morning to late morning

items.name: Pee Lek Herbal Fried Chicken (Khlong Toei Market)
items.blurb: A shop in the Khlong Toei Market area of Hat Yai, marinated with herbs until it's clearly fragrant, with crispy skin and meat that isn't greasy. It's a local spot people around Khlong Toei eat at regularly — not a social-media star, but consistent in flavor and good on price. Worth it if you're staying near or passing through this area and want fried chicken vouched for by the people who live there.
items.meta: Khlong Toei Market, Hat Yai · local shop

items.name: Jek Ob 3 Krata Fried Chicken (Saphan Dam junction)
items.blurb: A shop near the Saphan Dam junction whose selling point is no batter — fried so the marinade soaks straight into the meat, giving you bold flavor all the way through, with thin, crispy skin. For anyone who doesn't like thick, battered, heavy-skinned fried chicken, this one hits the spot. It's another local shop Hat Yai people know about but tourists usually don't.
items.meta: Near Saphan Dam junction · local shop

blocks.text: How to pick the shop that suits your taste

blocks.html: The easiest approach is to sort the shops by fried-chicken style and location first, then choose based on which area you're staying in that day. There's no need to drive across town for a single shop, because Hat Yai has great fried chicken spread all over — in the city center, in the markets, and out in the surrounding neighborhoods.

items: First time here, want a sure thing — Decha or Meena: easy to find, mild flavor, and you can have pulled tea or sticky rice all in one place.
Looking for original old-school / halal — Bang Jane near Khlong Rian, open 30 years, clearly garlicky.
Like bold, deeply marinated flavor — Sofiya on Si Uthit, or Jek Ob 3 Krata's no-batter style.
Cheap, snacky, late-night — Wanita at Chue Chang night market, or Pee Pla behind the hospital.
Staying near a market, want to walk over — Meena (Kim Yong), Sarina (Greenway), Malee (Si Trang).

blocks.title: Sticky rice and fried shallots are the stars
blocks.html: Hat Yai fried chicken that's genuinely good has to be eaten with hot sticky rice and crunchy fried shallots — the shallots add aroma and cut the richness. Don't forget to ask for more if the shop is stingy with them. Each shop's dipping sauce follows a different recipe, so dip a corner first before pouring it over the whole piece.

blocks.text: Prices, hours and what to know before you go

items: Price per piece — small wings start around 20–30 THB, while bigger thigh-and-drumstick pieces run up to 50–60 THB. Most sticky-rice-and-fried-chicken sets are around 50–70 THB.

Hours — some shops open late morning to evening (Decha, Meena), some are pushcarts that open late afternoon and sell out fast (Sofiya), and market shops usually sell in the morning to late morning. Check the hours before you leave your hotel.
Queues — popular shops like Pee Pla may hand out queue tickets, and weekend evenings get packed, so allow time to wait.
Cash — many pushcart and market shops take cash or PromptPay, so carrying small notes is more convenient.
Halal — if you need a halal shop, Bang Jane in Khlong Rian is a clear choice, and Sofiya is also a Muslim-run shop.

faq.q: Which Hat Yai fried chicken shops do locals actually eat at?
faq.a: Decha on Si Uthit Road is the busiest and the one locals mention most. The old halal shop Bang Jane near Khlong Rian has been selling for over 30 years, and the legendary Pee Pla behind Hat Yai Hospital is a spot Hat Yai people genuinely queue for. For your first shop, Decha and Meena (Kim Yong Market) are hard to get wrong.

faq.q: How much is Hat Yai fried chicken per piece?
faq.a: Small wings start around 20–30 THB, while bigger thigh-and-drumstick pieces run up to about 50–60 THB. If you order a sticky-rice-and-fried-chicken set, most are around 50–70 THB per set.

faq.q: How is Hat Yai fried chicken different from regular fried chicken?
faq.a: Hat Yai fried chicken is marinated with southern spices and herbs until the flavor soaks all the way into the meat. Some shops barely use batter, so it comes out with crispy skin and juicy meat, then gets topped with its signature crunchy fried shallots and eaten with sticky rice and a punchy dipping sauce — clearly different from the usual thick-battered fried chicken.

faq.q: Are there any halal Hat Yai fried chicken shops?
faq.a: Yes. Bang Jane near Khlong Rian Market is an old halal shop that's been around for over 30 years, and Sofiya on Si Uthit Road is a Muslim-run shop that also has khao mok (spiced rice) and chicken kolae to add on.

faq.q: What's the best time to go for Hat Yai fried chicken?
faq.a: It depends on the shop. Places like Decha and Meena open from late morning to evening, while pushcarts like Sofiya open in the late afternoon (around 3:30 pm) and often sell out fast. Many market shops sell in the morning to late morning. If you've got a popular shop in mind, check the opening hours and go before peak so you don't wait long in line.
